description: Rise on two feet, lower on one, five slow seconds down. Your heel drop count grades your Achilles under eccentric load, the exact stress tendons rebuild from. Here is the fifteen-rep line, the science of slow lowering, and the classic protocol behind it.

beats.text: STEP EDGE, ONE HAND ON THE WALL
UP ON TWO, DOWN ON ONE

lines: Anyone can rise. Few can descend.
beats.title: DOWN IS THE EXAM

scenes.narration: Stand on the edge of a step, heels hanging off, one hand resting on the wall for balance. Rise up onto your toes using both feet. Now lift one foot away, and lower yourself on the other leg, slowly, taking a full five seconds to sink until your heel is well below the step. That slow descent is one rep. Rise with two feet again, lower on one, and keep counting perfect five-second lowers until the descent speeds up, gets shaky, or you cannot control it anymore. Test both legs. That count is your heel drop score, and it grades something no other test in this season touches. Rising is the muscle's job, and almost everyone can rise. Lowering under control is the tendon's exam, because the Achilles has to brake your entire body weight while it is being stretched, rep after rep, with nowhere to hide. When the lowers get fast and jerky, the tendon has left the conversation and gravity is doing the reps. Keep your number, both legs. At the end of this video I will tell you what it reveals about the biggest tendon you own.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN DROPPING AND DESCENDING
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Fifteen perfect five-second, single-leg lowers is where a normal Achilles becomes a wired one. Under six controlled reps means the brakes are untrained, and that is the standard result for anyone who has only ever trained the rising half of movements. Six to fifteen means the tendon is learning to brake, and your descents will smooth out week by week. Over twenty-five per leg, you hold the level of eccentric control that tendon rehab programs aim for before they let athletes run and jump again. Respect the tempo rule, because it is the whole test. A two-second lower is not a slightly worse rep. It is a different, easier exam. Five honest seconds or the rep does not exist.
scenes.sub: under 6: brakes untrained - 6 to 15: building - over 25: rehab grade

scenes.narration: What you are doing in a heel drop has a name: eccentric loading. The muscle and tendon are producing force while they lengthen, like a rope brake lowering a heavy load hand over hand. This is the hardest job in the body, and the Achilles does it on every step you have ever taken, absorbing your landing before your calf fires you forward again. It is also, not coincidentally, the strongest rebuild signal a tendon knows. Decades of tendon research keep landing on the same finding: slow, heavy, eccentric work is what tells tendon tissue to reorganize its fibers, line them up along the load, and come back stiffer and stronger. The famous heel-drop programs that rescue painful Achilles tendons are built on exactly the movement you just tested, done slowly, twice a day, for months. So your count is not an internet stunt. It is a direct measure of the system those programs exist to rebuild, graded in the tendon's own language.

beats.title: SECONDS PER LOWER ACROSS THE SET

scenes.narration: Watch what actually fails during the test, because it is not what people expect. Your strength does not vanish at rep ten. Your tempo does. The lowers get a little faster, a little less smooth, and small jerks appear in the descent like static in a signal. That static is the measurement. Eccentric control is a coordination between the nervous system metering out force and the tendon transmitting it evenly while it stretches. When either side tires, the metering gets coarse, and gravity starts winning slices of the descent. This is why the five-second rule matters so much. Without a tempo standard, everyone passes this test and learns nothing. With it, the test becomes a truth serum for the exact quality that protects your Achilles in real life, because real landings are just heel drops that happen faster, when you are tired, on ground you did not inspect. The tendon that brakes smoothly in training is the one that brakes for you out there.

beats.text: THE SHAKY SIDE IS THE PRIORITY

scenes.narration: As always on this channel, the second number is hiding inside the first. Compare your legs. Most people find one descent that is smooth and one that stutters, and the stuttering side is rarely the one they expected. Brakes matter asymmetrically because life is asymmetrical: you land off curbs on one foot, you push off one leg to change direction, you catch yourself with whichever leg the moment chooses. The leg with the weak brake is the leg that will absorb the landing it was not ready for. If your counts differ by more than about a third, or one descent is visibly shakier at the same count, that side becomes the training priority. It goes first in every session, while the nervous system is fresh, and the strong leg matches its reps rather than setting them. This feels unfair to the strong leg for about two weeks. Then the gap closes, and both counts start climbing together, which is the pattern every test in this series keeps teaching: the body does not rise to its best link. It performs at its worst one, and it protects itself accordingly.

beats.text: YOUR WEIGHT IS THE MEDICINE DOSE

scenes.narration: Your advantage in this test is dosage. Eccentric Achilles work has a therapeutic window: heavy enough to signal rebuilding, light enough to stay controlled for fifteen slow reps. Heavy athletes blow through the top of that window on body weight alone, and their lowers turn into drops by rep five. Very deconditioned people never reach the window at all. You start inside it. Your body weight is almost exactly the medicine dose this tendon ordered, which means you can do more perfect reps, more days per week, with cleaner descents than almost anyone. That is why the classic heel-drop results, the ones from the original studies on stubborn Achilles pain, were achieved with nothing but body weight and a step. No machine, no plates, no gym. A step, a wall, and a frame light enough to descend honestly. You own all three already. The only missing ingredient is the schedule, and it is coming in one minute.
Now descend with me. Up on two feet, down on one, five slow seconds. Forty seconds per leg, twenty rest, three rounds. Smooth, no jerks. Go.

beats.text: TWICE A DAY, LIKE THE ORIGINAL PROGRAM
ADDING A BACKPACK IN WEEK ONE

scenes.narration: Here is your week, modeled on the original heel-drop program that changed Achilles rehab. Twice a day, three sets of fifteen slow lowers per leg, weak leg first, five seconds down, every single day. It sounds like a lot until you realize each session takes seven minutes and the tendon rebuilds on exactly this kind of relentless, boring schedule. After two weeks of perfect tempo, hold a light weight to add load. Three mistakes ruin this work. Counting fast drops as reps, which deletes the eccentric signal entirely. Loading a backpack in week one, before the brakes have learned control at body weight. And ignoring the tendon's feedback: a mild pull during the lowers is the program working, but sharp pain, morning stiffness that keeps worsening, or pain that changes how you walk means back off, and if Achilles pain persists, see a professional before you continue. This tendon carries you through every step of your life. Train it like it matters, because it does.

scenes.label: RETEST DAY - BOTH LEGS, SAME STEP
scenes.narration: So, your count. Under six per leg: the brakes are untrained, and untrained brakes on a light frame are the fastest climb in this season, because the dose is already perfect. Six to fifteen: you are building, and your job is tempo, twice a day, with zero drama. Over fifteen with smooth, silent descents on both sides: your Achilles is wired, and you own braking power that protects every landing in your future. Put both numbers in the comments, left and right. Just the numbers. We retest in thirty days, same step, same five seconds, and we watch the stutter disappear.
scenes.sub: under 6: brakes untrained - 6 to 15: building - over 15 even: wired

beats.text: FIVE SECONDS OR IT DIDN'T HAPPEN

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now, same step, same slow count, and we grade the brakes again. Subscribe, because next we leave the leg and test the tendon that ties your whole shoulder together. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Heel Drop Test Reveals the Truth About Your Achilles tendon
